blocks.title: First Sentences
blocks.subtitle: Say who and what things are

lessons.title: I am, you are
lessons.subtitle: Six pronouns and the verb 'to be'
lessons.grammarPointEn: Personal pronouns (man, tu, ō, mā, shumā, ānhā) with the present of 'to be': hastam, hasti, ast, hastēm, hastēd, hastand; the verb always comes last.

slides.title: Six little words
slides.body: Every Dari sentence starts with who it is about. These six pronouns cover everyone.

slides.title: The verb 'to be'
slides.body: Each pronoun pairs with its own form of 'to be'. Learn these six and you can already build real sentences.

slides.title: The verb goes last
slides.body: English says 'I am a teacher'. Dari says 'I teacher am' - the verb always closes the sentence.

lessons.title: This and that
lessons.subtitle: Point at the world with īn, ān, here and there
lessons.grammarPointEn: Demonstratives īn (this) and ān (that) with ast; the question īn chīst? (what is this?); īnjā (here) and ānjā (there).

slides.title: īn and ān
slides.body: īn points at something near you, ān at something far away. Both take ast, like ō.

slides.title: What is this?
slides.body: che (what) + ast squeezes into one word: chīst. It is the question you will ask most as a learner.

slides.title: Here and there
slides.body: īnjā means here, ānjā means there. They slot in right before the verb.

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.subtitle: Question words, yes and no
lessons.grammarPointEn: Question words che (what), kī (who), kujā (where), chetōr (how), chand (how many); yes/no questions are made by intonation alone and answered with balē (yes) or na (no).

slides.title: The question words
slides.body: Five words unlock most beginner questions. They sit where the answer would go - the verb still comes last.

slides.title: Yes or no
slides.body: To ask a yes/no question, keep the words exactly the same and raise your voice at the end. (In formal Dari you may hear āyā at the start.) Answer with balē - yes, or na - no.

blocks.title: Naming Things
blocks.subtitle: Plurals and the little -e that links words

lessons.title: More than one
lessons.subtitle: Make plurals with -hā
lessons.grammarPointEn: Plural nouns with the suffix -hā (ketāb → ketāb-hā); after a number the noun stays singular (dū ketāb, never dū ketāb-hā).

slides.title: Add -hā
slides.body: One suffix makes any noun plural: -hā. No exceptions to memorise.

slides.title: Numbers keep it singular
slides.body: After a number the noun never takes -hā. Literally: 'two book', 'three student'.

exercises.hint: After a number, the noun stays singular.

lessons.title: My, your, the teacher's
lessons.subtitle: Link owner and thing with ezāfa
lessons.grammarPointEn: Possession with the ezāfa linker -e / -ye: ketāb-e man (my book), khāna-ye mā (our house); the linker is spoken but usually not written in script.

slides.title: The invisible -e
slides.body: 'My book' is ketāb-e man - literally 'book of me'. The little -e (called ezāfa) is spoken but usually not written. After a vowel it becomes -ye.

slides.title: Chain it
slides.body: Keep linking with -e: khāna-ye padar-e man - 'my father's house'. Any owner works, not just pronouns.

lessons.title: Good friends, hot tea
lessons.subtitle: Describe things with ezāfa + adjective
lessons.grammarPointEn: Attributive adjectives follow the noun with ezāfa: dōst-e khōb (good friend), chāy-e garm (hot tea); chains like dōst-e khōb-e man (my good friend).

slides.title: Adjective after the noun
slides.body: In Dari the adjective follows its noun, linked by the same -e: chāy-e garm, 'tea of hot'.

slides.title: Chain it further
slides.body: Noun, adjective, owner - all linked with -e: dōst-e khōb-e man, 'my good friend'.

blocks.title: Where Things Are
blocks.subtitle: Little words of place, and saying what exists

lessons.title: In, to, from, with
lessons.subtitle: The four prepositions you'll use every day
lessons.grammarPointEn: Prepositions dar (in/at), ba (to), az (from), bā (with) placed before the noun: man dar kābul hastam (I am in Kabul).

slides.title: Before the noun
slides.body: Unlike the verb, prepositions work just like English: they come before their noun.

slides.title: Putting it together
slides.body: Combine prepositions with what you already know - questions, ezāfa, plurals.

distractorsEn: He is from my father's house.

lessons.title: There is, there isn't
lessons.subtitle: hast and nēst - saying what exists
lessons.grammarPointEn: Existential hast (there is) and nēst (there isn't) versus linking ast (is): dar khāna yak ketāb hast (there is a book in the house).

slides.title: hast - it exists
slides.body: hast says something exists; nēst says it doesn't. Perfect for what's in the house, the room, the market.

examples.en: There is a book in the house.
There is no water in the room.

slides.title: ast or hast?
slides.body: ast links two ideas - the tea IS hot. hast says something exists - there IS tea.

exercises.en: There is a book in the house.
There is no water in the room.
There is a teacher at the school.
distractorsEn: There is a student at the school.
There is no teacher at the school.

exercises.en: There is tea in the house.

blocks.title: Doing Things Now
blocks.subtitle: From having to doing - the present tense

lessons.title: I have two brothers
lessons.subtitle: dāshtan and counting to ten
lessons.grammarPointEn: The verb dāshtan (to have) in the present - dāram, dāri, dārad, dārēm, dārēd, dārand, with no mē- prefix - plus numbers and chand (how many).

slides.title: dāram - I have
slides.body: Your first real verb. The endings are the same family you met with hastam. dāshtan is special: no prefix needed in the present.

slides.title: Counting
slides.body: Numbers go before the noun - and remember, the noun stays singular.

examples.en: How many sisters do you have?

exercises.en: How many brothers do you have?

lessons.title: The mē- machine
lessons.subtitle: Say what you do with mē- + verb
lessons.grammarPointEn: Present tense: mē- + present stem + personal ending (mēkhānam, mēkhāni, mēkhānad, mēkhānēm, mēkhānēd, mēkhānand); the verb stays at the end of the sentence.

slides.title: The formula
slides.body: mē- + verb stem + the endings you know from dāram. That one pattern gives you the whole present tense.

slides.title: Four verbs to start
slides.body: Each verb has a present stem. Learn the stem and the formula does the rest.

slides.title: Still verb-last
slides.body: Subject, then everything else, then the verb. khurdan covers both eating and drinking.

lessons.title: The little word rā
lessons.subtitle: Mark the thing you act on
lessons.grammarPointEn: The object marker rā after definite direct objects: man ketāb rā mēkhānam (I read THE book) versus man ketāb mēkhānam (I read books in general).

slides.title: Spot the object
slides.body: When you act on a SPECIFIC thing - the book, that house - mark it with rā. Without rā it stays general.

slides.title: rā after the whole phrase
slides.body: rā comes after the complete object phrase, ezāfa chain and all.

lessons.title: Saying no
lessons.subtitle: namē-, nēstam and nadāram
lessons.grammarPointEn: Negation: namē- replaces mē- on present verbs (namērawam), 'to be' negates as nēstam/nēst, and dāshtan as nadāram.

slides.title: namē-
slides.body: Turn mē- into namē- and the sentence flips to 'don't'.

examples.en: He doesn't go to the bazaar.

slides.title: nēstam - I am not
slides.body: 'To be' has its own negative forms.

slides.title: nadāram - I don't have
slides.body: dāshtan takes plain na-: nadāram, nadāri, nadārad…

exercises.en: We don't go to the bazaar.
distractorsEn: We didn't go to the bazaar.

blocks.title: Talking About Yesterday
blocks.subtitle: The simple past and a victory lap

lessons.title: Yesterday I went
lessons.subtitle: The simple past
lessons.grammarPointEn: Simple past: past stem (infinitive minus -an) + endings -am, -ī, nothing, -ēm, -ēd, -and: raftam, raft, raftēm; time words dīrōz (yesterday), emrōz (today).

slides.title: Chop the -an
slides.body: raftan → raft. Add the same endings - except 'he/she', which takes nothing: ō raft. You can even drop the pronoun; the ending already says who.

examples.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

slides.title: Time words
slides.body: dīrōz - yesterday, emrōz - today, fardā - tomorrow. They usually open the sentence.

exercises.en: Yesterday I went to the bazaar.

lessons.title: Didn't - and done!
lessons.subtitle: Past negation, then everything together
lessons.grammarPointEn: Past negation with na- (nakardam, naraftam), plus mixed review of every A1 point: to be, plurals, ezāfa, prepositions, hast/nēst, dāshtan, present mē-, object rā, negation, and the simple past.

slides.title: na- + past
slides.body: The past negates with a simple na- in front: kardam → nakardam.

slides.title: You made it!
slides.body: That's the whole A1 toolkit: to be, plurals, ezāfa, prepositions, hast, dāshtan, the present, rā, negation and the past. These last exercises mix everything.

examples.target: من دری می‌خوانم و دیروز یک کتاب خواندم
examples.translit: man darī mēkhānam wa dīrōz yak ketāb khāndam
examples.en: I study Dari, and yesterday I read a book.

exercises.en: Yesterday I went to the city.
exercises.hint: You can drop the pronoun - the ending already says who.

exercises.en: There is no water in the house.

lessons.title: Bigger than that
lessons.subtitle: Comparatives with -tar and az
lessons.grammarPointEn: Comparative adjectives with the suffix -tar plus az (than): kalāntar az (bigger than); the compared thing follows az.

slides.title: Add -tar
slides.body: To compare, add -tar to the adjective: kalān → kalāntar (bigger), khōb → khōbtar (better in speech; bihtar is more common). The thing you compare against comes after az.

examples.target: خانه او از خانه من کلان‌تر است
examples.translit: khāna-ye ō az khāna-ye man kalāntar ast
examples.en: His house is bigger than my house.

slides.title: The order
slides.body: First the two things, joined by az, then the -tar adjective, then ast. Literally: 'X, from Y, bigger is.'

examples.target: کابل از شهر ما کلان‌تر است
examples.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast
examples.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.

exercises.target: این کتاب از آن کتاب ___ است
exercises.translit: īn ketāb az ān ketāb ___ ast
exercises.en: This book is newer than that book.

exercises.target: خانه او ___ خانه من کلان‌تر است
exercises.translit: khāna-ye ō ___ khāna-ye man kalāntar ast
exercises.en: His house is bigger than my house.

distractorsEn: Tea is as warm as water.

exercises.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.
exercises.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast

exercises.target: برادر من از تو کلان‌تر است
exercises.translit: barādar-e man az tu kalāntar ast
exercises.en: My brother is bigger than you.

distractorsTarget.target: برادر من از تو خوردتر است
distractorsTarget.translit: barādar-e man az tu khurdtar ast

distractorsTarget.target: برادر تو از من کلان‌تر است
distractorsTarget.translit: barādar-e tu az man kalāntar ast

lessons.title: The best of all
lessons.subtitle: Superlatives with -tarīn
lessons.grammarPointEn: Superlative adjectives with -tarīn, placed BEFORE the noun: bihtarīn dōst (the best friend), kalāntarīn shahr (the biggest city).

slides.title: Add -tarīn, move it front
slides.body: The superlative adds -tarīn - and unlike the adjective, it goes BEFORE the noun. bihtarīn is the special word for 'best'.

distractorsEn: He is a better friend than me.

lessons.title: My book, her name
lessons.subtitle: Possessive endings and khud
lessons.grammarPointEn: Attached possessive endings -am, -at, -ash, -emā, -etān, -eshān (ketābam = my book) as a shorter alternative to ketāb-e man; khud for 'own'.

slides.title: Stick it on the end
slides.body: Instead of ketāb-e man you can say ketābam - 'my book' - by attaching a short ending. Both are correct; the ending is quicker.

slides.title: khud - one's own
slides.body: khud means 'own' and works for any person: kār-e khud, 'one's own work'.

exercises.prompt: Match the two ways to say it

blocks.title: Time & Routine
blocks.subtitle: Clocks, habits, and what comes next

lessons.title: What time is it?
lessons.subtitle: Telling the hour
lessons.grammarPointEn: Telling time on the hour with sā'at: sā'at chand ast? (what time is it?), sā'at dū ast (it is two o'clock).

slides.title: sā'at + number
slides.body: sā'at means 'hour' or 'o'clock'. Ask sā'at chand ast? and answer with sā'at plus a number.

lessons.title: Always, sometimes, never
lessons.subtitle: How often you do things
lessons.grammarPointEn: Frequency expressions hamēsha (always), har rōz (every day), gāhē (sometimes), hargez + negative (never), placed before the verb.

slides.title: Where they go
slides.body: Frequency words sit before the verb: hamēsha (always), har rōz (every day), gāhē (sometimes). hargez means 'never' and pairs with a negative verb.

lessons.title: Tomorrow I'll go
lessons.subtitle: Talking about the future
lessons.grammarPointEn: Dari expresses the near future with the present tense plus a time word: fardā mērawam (tomorrow I go / will go); there is no separate everyday future tense.

slides.title: Present + time word
slides.body: For everyday plans, Dari uses the present tense with a future time word like fardā (tomorrow). No new verb form needed.

examples.en: Tomorrow I will go to Kabul.

exercises.en: Tomorrow I will go to Kabul.
Tomorrow we will read a book.
Tomorrow you will go to school.

lessons.title: Go! Read!
lessons.subtitle: The imperative
lessons.grammarPointEn: The imperative: be- + present stem (bura! = go!, bukhān! = read!); negative na- (naraw! = don't go!).

slides.title: be- + stem
slides.body: To give a command to one person, put be- on the present stem: raw → bura (go!), khān → bukhān (read!). For 'don't', use na-: naraw (don't go).

slides.title: Saying don't
slides.body: Swap be- for na- to forbid: naraw (don't go), nakhur (don't eat).

lessons.title: Please sit down
lessons.subtitle: Polite requests with the plural
lessons.grammarPointEn: Polite requests use the plural imperative (be- + stem + -ēd) with lutfan: lutfan bukhānēd (please read); the plural is polite even to one person.

slides.title: Add -ēd, add lutfan
slides.body: To be polite, use the plural command (be- + stem + -ēd) and start with lutfan (please). It is polite even when speaking to one person.

lessons.title: I want to go
lessons.subtitle: mēkhāham + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: mēkhāham (I want) plus a second verb in the subjunctive (be- form): mēkhāham burawam (I want to go); the second verb has no mē-.

slides.title: Want + a second verb
slides.body: 'I want to go' uses two verbs: mēkhāham (I want) + burawam (go). This second form - be- + stem + ending - is the 'want-form' (subjunctive). It never takes mē-.

exercises.en: I want to read a book.
We want to go to the bazaar.

lessons.title: I can read
lessons.subtitle: mētawānam + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: mētawānam (I can) plus a second verb in the subjunctive: mētawānam bukhānam (I can read); same be- form as with 'want'.

slides.title: Can + a second verb
slides.body: 'Can' works just like 'want': mētawānam (I can) + the be- form. mētawānam bukhānam - 'I can read'.

lessons.title: I must go
lessons.subtitle: bāyad + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: bāyad (must) with the subjunctive: bāyad burawam (I must go); bāyad does not change form for person.

slides.title: bāyad never changes
slides.body: bāyad means 'must'. Unlike other verbs it stays the same for everyone - only the second verb (the be- form) changes for person.

blocks.title: Experiences & Joining Ideas
blocks.subtitle: The past deepens; sentences join up

lessons.title: I used to go
lessons.subtitle: Past habits with mē- + past
lessons.grammarPointEn: Past habitual/continuous: mē- on the simple past (mēraftam = I used to go / I was going), for repeated or ongoing past actions.

slides.title: mē- on the past
slides.body: Put mē- on a past-tense verb to say you 'used to' do it, or 'were' doing it: raftam (I went) → mēraftam (I used to go).

examples.en: I used to go to school every day.
He always used to drink tea.

exercises.en: I used to go to school every day.
He always used to eat bread.
I sometimes used to go to the bazaar.
You used to work every day.

lessons.title: I have gone
lessons.subtitle: The present perfect
lessons.grammarPointEn: Present perfect: past participle (past stem + -a) plus a short ending (rafta-am = I have gone); 3rd person is rafta ast.

slides.title: Participle + ending
slides.body: For 'I have done' something, take the participle (rafta, khurda) and add a short ending. For 'he has', it is participle + ast.

lessons.title: Doing and making
lessons.subtitle: Compound verbs with kardan
lessons.grammarPointEn: Compound verbs = noun + kardan: kār kardan (to work), zendagī kardan (to live), fikr kardan (to think), kumak kardan (to help); only kardan conjugates.

slides.title: Noun + kardan
slides.body: Many Dari verbs are a noun plus kardan. Only kardan changes; the noun stays put. kār kardan (work), fikr kardan (think), kumak kardan (help).

lessons.title: I know that…
lessons.subtitle: Joining sentences with ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: The conjunction ke (that) joins a main verb of thinking/saying to a full clause: mēdānam ke ō āmad (I know that he came).

slides.title: ke links two ideas
slides.body: Use ke (that) after verbs like 'know', 'say', 'think' to attach a whole sentence: guftam ke mērawam - 'I said that I am going'.

examples.en: I said that I am going to the bazaar.

exercises.en: I said that I am going to the bazaar.
distractorsEn: He said that he is going to the bazaar.

exercises.en: I think that he is a teacher.
exercises.translit: fikr mēkunam ke ō mu'allem ast

exercises.en: He said that he ate bread.
He knows that I am here.

lessons.title: A2 review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from this level, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of A2: comparatives, superlatives, possessive endings, telling time, frequency, future, imperative, modals with the subjunctive, past habitual, present perfect, compound verbs, and ke-clauses.

slides.title: You've come far
slides.body: You can now compare things, give commands, say what you want and must do, talk about habits and experiences, and join ideas with ke. These exercises mix it all.

examples.en: I want to go to the best city.

exercises.target: خانه او از خانه من ___ است
exercises.translit: khāna-ye ō az khāna-ye man ___ ast
exercises.en: His house is bigger than my house.

exercises.target: می‌دانم که او بهترین دوست من است
exercises.translit: mēdānam ke ō bihtarīn dōst-e man ast
exercises.en: I know that he is my best friend.

distractorsTarget.target: می‌دانم که او دوست من است
distractorsTarget.translit: mēdānam ke ō dōst-e man ast

distractorsTarget.target: فکر می‌کنم که او بهترین دوست من است
distractorsTarget.translit: fikr mēkunam ke ō bihtarīn dōst-e man ast

blocks.title: The Subjunctive System
blocks.subtitle: The be- form, on its own terms

lessons.title: The be- form in full
lessons.subtitle: Subjunctive for every person
lessons.grammarPointEn: The present subjunctive: be- + present stem + personal endings, used after modals, wishes and purpose; the verb drops mē-. Negative is na- + stem.

slides.title: One form, many uses
slides.body: You met the be- form after want/can/must. It is the subjunctive, and it appears whenever an action is wished, needed, or not yet real. It never takes mē-.

slides.title: Saying not
slides.body: The negative subjunctive uses na-: narawam (that I not go), nabāsham (that I not be).

examples.en: It is better that you don't go.

exercises.en: It is better that you don't go.
distractorsEn: It is better that you go.
It was better that you went.

exercises.hint: After bāyad, the verb takes the be- form, not mē-.

exercises.en: I want you to read the book.
It is possible that he comes.

lessons.title: Maybe he'll come
lessons.subtitle: shāyad and mumkin ast
lessons.grammarPointEn: Expressing possibility with shāyad (maybe) and mumkin ast (it's possible) followed by the subjunctive: shāyad biāyad (maybe he'll come).

slides.title: Possibility takes the be- form
slides.body: Because a possibility is not yet real, shāyad (maybe) and mumkin ast (it is possible that) are followed by the subjunctive.

exercises.hint: After shāyad, use the be- form.

lessons.title: So that I can buy bread
lessons.subtitle: Purpose with tā and ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Purpose clauses with tā or ke ('so that', 'in order to') taking the subjunctive: raftam tā nān bukharam (I went to buy bread).

slides.title: Why you did it
slides.body: To say why you do something, use tā (or ke) + the subjunctive: 'I went so that I could buy bread'. tā here means 'in order to'.

examples.target: به بازار رفتم تا نان بخرم
examples.translit: ba bāzār raftam tā nān bukharam
examples.en: I went to the bazaar to buy bread.

exercises.en: I went to the bazaar to buy bread.

distractorsEn: I will come to see you.

exercises.en: He went to the school to study.
exercises.translit: ba maktab raft tā dars bukhānad

exercises.en: I came in order to work.
exercises.hint: After tā (in order to), use the be- form.

exercises.target: به خانه رفتم تا چای بخورم
exercises.translit: ba khāna raftam tā chāy bukhuram
exercises.en: I went home to drink tea.

distractorsTarget.target: به خانه رفتم و چای خوردم
distractorsTarget.translit: ba khāna raftam wa chāy khurdam

distractorsTarget.target: به خانه می‌روم تا چای بخورم
distractorsTarget.translit: ba khāna mērawam tā chāy bukhuram

exercises.en: I bought a book to read.

lessons.title: If you go…
lessons.subtitle: Real conditions with agar
lessons.grammarPointEn: Real (possible) conditionals: agar + subjunctive in the if-clause, present tense in the result clause: agar burawi, ō rā mēbīni (if you go, you'll see him).

slides.title: agar + be- form
slides.body: For a real, possible condition, use agar (if) with the subjunctive, and the present tense for the result. 'If you go, you'll see him.'

examples.en: If you go, you will see him.
If it rains, we won't go.

exercises.en: If you go, you will see him.
If it rains, we won't go.
distractorsEn: It rained, so we didn't go.

exercises.target: اگر تو می‌آیی، من خوش می‌شوم
exercises.translit: agar tu mēāyi, man khush mēshawam
exercises.en: If you come, I'll be happy.
exercises.hint: After agar, the if-verb takes the be- form.

exercises.en: If you study, you will learn.
If I have time, I'll come.
If he comes, I'll be happy.

lessons.title: When he came…
lessons.subtitle: Time clauses with waqtē ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Time clauses with waqtē ke (when): waqtē ke āmad, khāna būdam (when he came, I was at home); a past time-clause takes the past tense.

slides.title: waqtē ke - when
slides.body: waqtē ke means 'when' and joins two events. For past events, both verbs are in the past.

examples.target: وقتی که آمد، من خانه بودم
examples.translit: waqtē ke āmad, man khāna būdam
examples.en: When he came, I was at home.

exercises.en: When he came, I was at home.

exercises.target: وقتی که او رفت، ما آمدیم
exercises.translit: waqtē ke ō raft, mā āmadēm
distractorsEn: He left and we didn't come.

exercises.en: When I saw him, I was happy.
exercises.translit: waqtē ke ō rā dīdam, khush shudam

exercises.target: وقتی که نان خوردم، به مکتب رفتم
exercises.translit: waqtē ke nān khurdam, ba maktab raftam
exercises.en: When I had eaten, I went to school.

distractorsTarget.target: نان خوردم و به مکتب می‌روم
distractorsTarget.translit: nān khurdam wa ba maktab mērawam

distractorsTarget.target: وقتی که نان می‌خورم، به مکتب می‌روم
distractorsTarget.translit: waqtē ke nān mēkhuram, ba maktab mērawam

lessons.title: I had already gone
lessons.subtitle: The past perfect
lessons.grammarPointEn: Past perfect: past participle + budam/būdi/būd… (rafta būdam = I had gone), for an action completed before another past moment.

slides.title: Participle + būdam
slides.body: For 'I had done' something before another past event, use the participle + the past of budan: rafta būdam - 'I had gone'.

examples.target: وقتی که آمدی، من رفته بودم
examples.translit: waqtē ke āmadi, man rafta būdam
examples.en: When you came, I had already gone.

exercises.en: When you came, I had already gone.

exercises.target: وقتی که من آمدم، او رفته است
exercises.translit: waqtē ke man āmadam, ō rafta ast
exercises.en: When I came, he had gone.
exercises.hint: A past-before-past uses būd (had), not ast (has).

lessons.title: Went, or have gone?
lessons.subtitle: Simple past vs present perfect
lessons.grammarPointEn: Contrast between the simple past (a finished moment: raftam) and present perfect (experience or relevance now: rafta-am).

slides.title: Two kinds of past
slides.body: raftam points to a specific finished moment ('I went yesterday'). rafta-am points to experience or result now ('I have been there'). Time words like dīrōz go with the simple past.

exercises.hint: With dīrōz (yesterday), use the simple past.
dīrōz names a finished moment, so use the simple past.

lessons.title: First, then, after that
lessons.subtitle: Telling a story in order
lessons.grammarPointEn: Sequencing a past narrative with awal (first), bād (then/after), and bād az ān (after that), all with the simple past.

slides.title: Ordering events
slides.body: String past events together with awal (first), bād (then), bād az ān (after that). Keep the verbs in the simple past.

examples.target: اول نان خوردم، بعد به مکتب رفتم
examples.translit: awal nān khurdam, bād ba maktab raftam
examples.en: First I ate, then I went to school.

exercises.en: First I ate, then I left.

exercises.target: اول کار کردم، بعد از آن چای خوردم
exercises.translit: awal kār kardam, bād az ān chāy khurdam
exercises.en: First I worked, after that I drank tea.
distractorsEn: First I drank tea, then I worked.
I work, then I drink tea.

exercises.en: First he came, then he sat.
I ate, then I went to the bazaar.
First I studied, then I slept.

blocks.title: Connecting Ideas
blocks.subtitle: Clauses that describe, report, and explain

lessons.title: The man who came
lessons.subtitle: Relative clauses with ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Relative clauses: an indefinite noun marked with -ē plus ke introduces a describing clause: mardē ke āmad (the man who came), ketābē ke khāndam (the book that I read).

slides.title: noun + ‑ē + ke
slides.body: To say 'the man who…' or 'the book that…', add ‑ē to the noun and follow with ke and a clause. The ‑ē signals 'the particular one that…'.

examples.target: مردی که آمد، دوست من است
examples.translit: mardē ke āmad, dōst-e man ast
examples.en: The man who came is my friend.
The book that I read was good.

exercises.en: The man who came is my friend.
The book that I read was good.
distractorsEn: I read a good book today.

exercises.en: The woman who came is a teacher.

exercises.target: شهری را که دیدم، کلان بود
exercises.translit: shahrē rā ke dīdam, kalān būd
exercises.en: The city that I saw was big.
exercises.hint: A relative clause opens with ke; here rā does not belong.

exercises.en: The house that I saw was beautiful.

lessons.title: He said that…
lessons.subtitle: Reporting what people say
lessons.grammarPointEn: Reported speech with ke: guft ke mērawad (he said that he is going); unlike English, the reported verb's tense does not shift back.

slides.title: Keep the tense
slides.body: Report speech with ke. Dari keeps the original tense: 'He said that he IS going' (not 'was going'). The verb stays as first spoken.

examples.en: He said that he is going.
He said that he ate bread.

exercises.en: He said that he is going.
He said that he ate bread.
She said that she is a teacher.
He said that he will come tomorrow.
I said that I am working.

lessons.title: Because and but
lessons.subtitle: Cause and contrast
lessons.grammarPointEn: Joining ideas by cause and contrast: chun / zērā (because), amā / walē (but); the clause order and meaning they create.

slides.title: Why and yet
slides.body: chun and zērā both mean 'because'. amā and walē both mean 'but'. They link two full clauses.

examples.en: I didn't go because I was sick.
I ate but I am tired.

exercises.en: I didn't go because I was sick.
I ate but I am tired.
distractorsEn: I ate because I am tired.
I am tired, so I ate.

exercises.target: می‌روم چون او را نمی‌بینم اما دوست دارم
exercises.translit: mērawam chun ō rā namēbīnam amā dōst dāram
exercises.en: I go because I don't see him, but I like him.
exercises.hint: The first join is a contrast, not a cause.

exercises.en: I came because I like you.
exercises.translit: āmadam chun tu rā dōst dāram

exercises.en: I worked but I am not tired.

lessons.title: It was written
lessons.subtitle: The passive with shudan
lessons.grammarPointEn: Passive voice with the past participle + shudan: neweshta shud (it was written), dīda mēshawad (it is seen); no doer is named.

slides.title: participle + shudan
slides.body: To say something 'was done' without naming who did it, use the participle + a form of shudan (to become): neweshta shud - 'it was written'.

exercises.hint: The passive uses shudan (to become), not kardan.

lessons.title: A certain book
lessons.subtitle: The indefinite -ē
lessons.grammarPointEn: The indefinite -ē (yā-ye wahdat) marks 'a certain / some': ketābē kharīdam (I bought a book); contrasts with a bare noun or with yak.

slides.title: Add -ē for 'a certain'
slides.body: Attaching -ē to a noun means 'a certain one': ketābē (a book), rōzē (one day). It is softer than yak and common in storytelling.

examples.en: One day I went to the bazaar.

exercises.en: One day I went to Kabul.
distractorsEn: Every day I go to Kabul.

lessons.title: Every, none, all
lessons.subtitle: Quantifiers
lessons.grammarPointEn: Quantifiers har (every, + singular), hēch (no/none, + negative verb), hama (all), kasē (someone), chīzē (something).

slides.title: How much, how many
slides.body: har (every) takes a singular noun; hama means 'all'; hēch means 'no/none' and needs a negative verb; kasē / chīzē mean 'someone / something'.

exercises.hint: hēch (none) needs a negative verb.
With hēch, the verb must be negative.

lessons.title: He will go
lessons.subtitle: The formal future with khāhad
lessons.grammarPointEn: Formal future: khāham/khāhi/khāhad… + the bare past stem (khāham raft = I will go); common in writing and formal speech, alongside the everyday present-as-future.

slides.title: khāhad + past stem
slides.body: In formal or written Dari, the future is khāham (etc.) + the bare past stem: khāham raft - 'I will go'. In everyday speech, the present tense with a time word is more common.

lessons.title: Building new words
lessons.subtitle: The -ī that makes nouns
lessons.grammarPointEn: Word formation: the suffix -ī turns adjectives into abstract nouns (āzād → āzādī 'freedom', zenda → zendagī 'life'); recognizing built words widens vocabulary.

slides.title: The -ī of ideas
slides.body: A final -ī often turns a word into an abstract idea: āzād (free) → āzādī (freedom), zenda (alive) → zendagī (life). Spotting the pattern helps you guess new words.

exercises.en: The people of this city are good.

lessons.title: B1 review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from this level, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of B1: the subjunctive after modals, possibility and purpose; real conditionals; when-clauses; past perfect; simple past vs present perfect; relative clauses; reported speech; cause and contrast; the passive; the indefinite -ē; quantifiers; and the formal future.

slides.title: You can say a lot now
slides.body: You can hypothesize, report, describe with clauses, and shift between layers of past. These exercises mix it all - watch for the subtle mistakes.

examples.target: اگر بیایی، مردی را که دیدم می‌بینی
examples.translit: agar biāyi, mardē rā ke dīdam mēbīni
examples.en: If you come, you'll see the man I saw.

exercises.en: If you come, I'll be happy.
exercises.hint: After agar, the if-verb takes the be- form.

exercises.en: He said that he will come tomorrow.

exercises.target: وقتی که آمدی، من رفته بودم
exercises.translit: waqtē ke āmadi, man rafta būdam
exercises.en: When you came, I had already gone.

exercises.hint: The passive uses shudan.

exercises.en: The book that I read was good.

lessons.title: If I had known
lessons.subtitle: Counterfactual conditionals
lessons.grammarPointEn: Counterfactual (unreal) conditionals: agar + mē- past in the if-clause and mē- past in the result: agar mēdānistam, namēraftam (if I had known, I wouldn't have gone).

slides.title: Unreal uses mē- past
slides.body: For something contrary to fact - that didn't actually happen - both clauses use the mē- past. 'If I had known (but I didn't), I wouldn't have gone.'

examples.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.

slides.title: Real vs unreal
slides.body: Compare: agar burawi (if you go - still possible) with agar mērafti (if you had gone - but you didn't). The mē- past signals 'unreal'.

examples.en: If I had had time, I would have come.

exercises.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.
If I had had time, I would have come.
distractorsEn: If I have time, I'll come.
I had time and I came.

exercises.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.
exercises.hint: The unreal result also takes the mē- past.

exercises.en: If you had come, you would have seen him.
If I had had money, I would have bought a book.

distractorsTarget.target: اگر پول داشته باشم، کتاب می‌خرم
distractorsTarget.translit: agar pūl dāshta bāsham, ketāb mēkharam

exercises.en: If he had come, we would have been happy.

lessons.title: If only he came
lessons.subtitle: Wishes and regrets with kāsh
lessons.grammarPointEn: Wishes with kāsh (if only) + mē- past for an unfulfilled present/future wish: kāsh mēāmad (if only he would come / had come).

slides.title: kāsh + mē- past
slides.body: kāsh means 'if only'. For a wish that isn't reality, follow it with the mē- past: kāsh mēāmad - 'if only he would come'.

exercises.hint: A wish that isn't real takes the mē- past.

exercises.en: If only I had more time.

lessons.title: He may have gone
lessons.subtitle: The past subjunctive
lessons.grammarPointEn: Past subjunctive: past participle + bāsham/bāshi/bāshad… (rafta bāsham), used after shāyad, mumkin, and doubt about a past event.

slides.title: participle + bāshad
slides.body: To talk about a past action you're unsure of, use the participle + the subjunctive of budan (bāshad): shāyad rafta bāshad - 'maybe he has gone'.

exercises.target: ممکن است که نان خورده باشد
exercises.translit: mumken ast ke nān khurda bāshad

exercises.hint: Doubt about the past takes bāshad, not ast.

exercises.en: Maybe you have read the book.

lessons.title: One can say
lessons.subtitle: Impersonal mētawān
lessons.grammarPointEn: The impersonal mētawān + short infinitive expresses 'one can / it is possible to': mētawān guft (one can say); no subject is named.

slides.title: mētawān + short infinitive
slides.body: For 'one can' or 'it is possible to', use mētawān with a short infinitive (the past stem): mētawān guft - 'one can say'. It has no personal ending.

examples.target: می‌توان گفت که او خوب است
examples.translit: mētawān guft ke ō khōb ast
examples.en: One can say that he is good.

exercises.en: One can say that he is good.
One can see that he came.
exercises.hint: The impersonal form has no personal ending.

lessons.title: Passive, any tense
lessons.subtitle: shudan across time
lessons.grammarPointEn: The passive across tenses by conjugating shudan: neweshta mēshawad (is written), neweshta shud (was written), neweshta shuda ast (has been written).

slides.title: Move shudan through time
slides.body: The participle stays; only shudan changes tense: mēshawad (is done), shud (was done), shuda ast (has been done).

exercises.hint: The passive uses shudan, so 'is written' is mēshawad.

lessons.title: He must have gone
lessons.subtitle: Deduction about the past
lessons.grammarPointEn: Deduction about the past: bāyad + past participle + bāshad (bāyad rafta bāshad = he must have gone) for a confident conclusion.

slides.title: bāyad + participle + bāshad
slides.body: To conclude that something surely happened, combine bāyad (must) with the past subjunctive: bāyad rafta bāshad - 'he must have gone'.

exercises.hint: Deduction about the past ends in bāshad, not the plain subjunctive.

exercises.target: او باید کتاب را خوانده باشد
exercises.translit: ō bāyad ketāb rā khānda bāshad
exercises.en: He must have read the book.

lessons.title: The very book that…
lessons.subtitle: Advanced relative clauses
lessons.grammarPointEn: Relative clauses with a definite antecedent using ān … ke and resumptive structure: ān ketābē ke khāndam (that book which I read); distinguishing defining from adding information.

slides.title: ān … ke
slides.body: To point precisely, frame the noun with ān (that) and close with ke: ān mardē ke dīdam - 'that man whom I saw'. The clause narrows down exactly which one.

examples.target: آن کتابی که خواندم، مقبول بود
examples.translit: ān ketābē ke khāndam, maqbūl būd
examples.en: That book which I read was beautiful.

exercises.en: That man whom I saw was a teacher.

exercises.target: آن کتابی که خواندم، مقبول بود
exercises.translit: ān ketābē ke khāndam, maqbūl būd
exercises.en: That book which I read was beautiful.
distractorsEn: A book I read was beautiful.
That beautiful book, I read it.

exercises.en: The city that I saw was big.
exercises.translit: ān shahrē ke dīdam, kalān būd

exercises.target: آن دوستی را که آمد، دیدم
exercises.translit: ān dōstē rā ke āmad, dīdam
exercises.en: I saw that friend who came.
exercises.hint: The subject of the relative clause takes ke directly, not rā.

exercises.target: آن خانه‌ای که خریدم، کلان است
exercises.translit: ān khāna-ē ke kharīdam, kalān ast
exercises.en: That house which I bought is big.
That book which I read was good.

lessons.title: Even though
lessons.subtitle: Concession with harchand
lessons.grammarPointEn: Concessive clauses with harchand (even though) and bā wujūd-e īn (despite this), granting a point before contrasting it.

slides.title: harchand … but
slides.body: harchand means 'even though'. It opens a clause you concede, before a contrasting main clause, often with amā.

examples.en: Even though he was tired, he worked.

exercises.en: Even though he was tired, he worked.
Even though it was raining, we went.
distractorsEn: Because it was raining, we went.

exercises.en: Even though he was sick, he came.
Even though it is big, it is cheap.

exercises.target: چون مانده بود، اما کار کرد
exercises.translit: chun mānda būd, amā kār kard
exercises.en: Even though he was tired, he worked.
exercises.hint: A conceded point uses harchand, not chun (because).

lessons.title: Until, as soon as
lessons.subtitle: The many senses of tā
lessons.grammarPointEn: The word tā across senses: 'until' (tā ke), 'as soon as', and 'so that' (purpose); reading which meaning from context.

slides.title: One word, three jobs
slides.body: tā can mean 'in order to' (with the subjunctive), 'until' (with a limit), or 'as soon as'. The verb form and context tell you which.

examples.target: تا او را دیدم، خوش شدم
examples.translit: tā ō rā dīdam, khush shudam
examples.en: As soon as I saw him, I was happy.

exercises.target: تا او را دیدم، خوش شدم
exercises.translit: tā ō rā dīdam, khush shudam
exercises.en: As soon as I saw him, I was happy.
distractorsEn: Until I saw him, I was happy.
I saw him so that I'd be happy.

exercises.en: As soon as he came, we left.
Wait so that I can eat.

lessons.title: While and the moment that
lessons.subtitle: Simultaneous actions
lessons.grammarPointEn: Simultaneous actions with dar hālē ke (while) and hamīn ke (the moment that), joining two overlapping events.

slides.title: At the same time
slides.body: dar hālē ke means 'while' - two things at once. hamīn ke means 'the moment that' - one triggers the other.

examples.target: در حالی که نان می‌خوردم، او آمد
examples.translit: dar hālē ke nān mēkhurdam, ō āmad
examples.en: While I was eating, he came.

exercises.target: در حالی که نان می‌خوردم، او آمد
exercises.translit: dar hālē ke nān mēkhurdam, ō āmad
exercises.en: While I was eating, he came.
distractorsEn: Because I was eating, he came.

exercises.target: ___ که او را دیدم، خوش شدم
exercises.translit: ___ ke ō rā dīdam, khush shudam
exercises.en: The moment I saw him, I was happy.
While I was reading, he slept.
exercises.translit: dar hālē ke mēkhāndam, ō khābīd

exercises.en: The moment he came, we left.
While I was eating, he came.
exercises.hint: Two actions at once use 'while', not 'because'.

lessons.title: Written and spoken
lessons.subtitle: Register in Dari
lessons.grammarPointEn: Recognizing register: formal/written forms (ast, mērawad, endings intact) versus everyday spoken shapes; choosing what fits the situation.

slides.title: Two ways to say it
slides.body: Written Dari keeps full forms - ō mērawad ast style. Spoken Kabuli often shortens them. Knowing both lets you read and speak naturally. In this course we teach the clear, full forms.

exercises.en: They go to the bazaar. (full form)

lessons.title: The act of going
lessons.subtitle: Verbs used as nouns
lessons.grammarPointEn: Nominalization: the infinitive used as a noun (raftan = going / to go), often with ezāfa (raftan-e ō = his going) or after barāye (barāye khāndan = for reading).

slides.title: The infinitive as a noun
slides.body: The infinitive (raftan, khāndan) can act as a noun: 'going', 'reading'. Use it after barāye (for) or with ezāfa: barāye khāndan - 'for reading'.

examples.en: I came in order to read.

exercises.target: رفتن او من را خوش نکرد
exercises.translit: raftan-e ō man rā khush nakard
exercises.en: His going did not make me happy.

distractorsTarget.target: او رفت و من خوش نشدم
distractorsTarget.translit: ō raft wa man khush nashudam

distractorsTarget.target: رفتن من او را خوش کرد
distractorsTarget.translit: raftan-e man ō rā khush kard

lessons.title: Words built from words
lessons.subtitle: Compounds and the -gī noun
lessons.grammarPointEn: Word formation: ham- 'co-' compounds (hamkār = colleague, hamsenf = classmate) and the -gī ending that makes nouns from words ending in -a (zenda → zendagī).

slides.title: ham- = together
slides.body: The prefix ham- means 'co-' or 'fellow': hamkār (co-worker), hamsenf (classmate). Spotting ham- unlocks many words at once.

slides.title: -gī makes ideas
slides.body: Words ending in -a take -gī to become abstract nouns: zenda (alive) → zendagī (life).

examples.en: Life in the village is calm.

exercises.en: Life in the village is calm.
distractorsEn: He lives in the calm village.

lessons.title: He told me that…
lessons.subtitle: Reported speech, deeper
lessons.grammarPointEn: Reported speech across frames: reporting questions and commands with ke and the subjunctive; the reported tense still does not shift back as in English.

slides.title: Reporting asks and orders
slides.body: To report a request or command, use ke + the subjunctive: guft ke burawam - 'he told me to go'. To report a question, keep the question word after ke.

examples.en: He asked where I was going.

distractorsEn: He said that he is going.

exercises.en: He asked where I was going.
The teacher told me to study.
exercises.hint: A reported command takes the subjunctive.

lessons.title: Therefore, on one hand
lessons.subtitle: Discourse connectors
lessons.grammarPointEn: Higher-level connectors that structure a paragraph: binābar'īn (therefore), az yak taraf … az taraf-e dīgar (on one hand … on the other).

slides.title: Signposting your ideas
slides.body: These connectors organise longer speech: binābar'īn (therefore) draws a conclusion; az yak taraf … az taraf-e dīgar weighs two sides.

examples.en: I was tired, therefore I didn't go.

exercises.en: I was tired, therefore I didn't go.
It was raining, therefore we stayed home.
distractorsEn: It was raining, but we stayed home.
If it rains, we stay home.

exercises.en: He was sick, therefore he didn't come.

exercises.target: او کار کرد، بنابراین مانده است
exercises.translit: ō kār kard, binābar'īn mānda ast
exercises.en: He worked, therefore he is tired.

distractorsTarget.target: او کار کرد اما مانده است
distractorsTarget.translit: ō kār kard amā mānda ast

distractorsTarget.target: او مانده است چون کار می‌کند
distractorsTarget.translit: ō mānda ast chun kār mēkunad

exercises.en: I was tired, therefore I didn't go.
exercises.hint: This draws a conclusion - 'therefore', not 'if'.

lessons.title: B2 review
lessons.subtitle: The whole journey, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of B2: counterfactual conditionals, wishes, the past subjunctive, impersonal mētawān, the passive across tenses, deduction, advanced relative clauses, concession, tā and simultaneity, register, nominalization, word formation, reported speech and discourse connectors.

slides.title: You've reached B2
slides.body: You can now hypothesise about the unreal, hedge about the past, structure an argument, and shift register. This final set draws on everything - read closely.

examples.target: اگر می‌دانستم که آمده است، صبر می‌کردم
examples.translit: agar mēdānistam ke āmada ast, sabr mēkardam
examples.en: If I had known he had come, I would have waited.

exercises.en: If I had known, I wouldn't have gone.
exercises.hint: The unreal result takes the mē- past.

exercises.target: چون مانده بود، اما کار کرد
exercises.translit: chun mānda būd, amā kār kard
exercises.en: Even though he was tired, he worked.
exercises.hint: A conceded point uses harchand.

exercises.en: That book which I read was good.
exercises.translit: ān ketābē ke khāndam, khōb būd

exercises.en: I was tired, therefore I didn't go.

lessons.title: Although, and still
lessons.subtitle: Concession with agarche
lessons.grammarPointEn: Concession with agarche / garche (although) answered by bāz ham (still, even so) in the main clause: agarche mānda būd, bāz ham kār kard.

slides.title: agarche … bāz ham
slides.body: agarche (although) opens a conceded fact; the main clause often answers with bāz ham (still). Together they sharpen a contrast beyond a plain amā.

examples.target: اگرچه مانده بود، باز هم کار کرد
examples.translit: agarche mānda būd, bāz ham kār kard
examples.en: Although he was tired, he still worked.

exercises.target: ___ مانده بود، باز هم کار کرد
exercises.translit: ___ mānda būd, bāz ham kār kard
exercises.en: Although he was tired, he still worked.

exercises.target: گرچه باران بود، باز هم رفتیم
exercises.translit: garche bārān būd, bāz ham raftēm
exercises.en: Although it was raining, we still went.
distractorsEn: Because it was raining, we went.
If it rains, we still go.

exercises.target: چون مریض بود، باز هم آمد
exercises.translit: chun marīz būd, bāz ham āmad
exercises.en: Although he was sick, he still came.
exercises.hint: 'Although' concedes a point; chun means 'because'.

exercises.en: Although it was cold, we went to the bazaar.
exercises.translit: agarche sard būd, ba bāzār raftēm

exercises.en: Although he had no money, he bought a book.

lessons.title: Unless, or else
lessons.subtitle: magar and wa gar na
lessons.grammarPointEn: Exclusion and warning: magar (unless / except) and wa gar na (otherwise), which introduce a consequence if a condition fails.

slides.title: The escape clauses
slides.body: magar means 'unless' or 'except'. wa gar na means 'otherwise' - it warns what happens if the first clause isn't met.

examples.en: I won't go unless you come.

examples.translit: zūd biā, wa gar na mērawēm

exercises.en: I won't go unless you come.

exercises.translit: zūd biā, wa gar na mērawēm
distractorsEn: Come soon, because we are going.
Come soon so that we go.

exercises.translit: bukhāb, wa gar na mānda mēshawi

exercises.en: I won't come unless you go.
exercises.hint: 'Unless' is magar, not 'although'.

exercises.translit: kār kun, wa gar na pūl namēgīri
exercises.en: Work, otherwise you won't get money.

lessons.title: On the condition that
lessons.subtitle: Stipulating with ba shart-ē ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Stipulating a condition with ba shart-ē ke (on the condition that) + subjunctive: mēāyam ba shart-ē ke tu ham biāyi.

slides.title: Setting a term
slides.body: ba shart-ē ke means 'on the condition that' and takes the subjunctive. It states a precise term for agreeing to something.

examples.target: می‌آیم به شرطی که تو هم بیایی
examples.translit: mēāyam ba shart-ē ke tu ham biāyi
examples.en: I'll come, on the condition that you come too.

exercises.target: می‌آیم به شرطی که تو هم ___
exercises.translit: mēāyam ba shart-ē ke tu ham ___
exercises.en: I'll come, on the condition that you come too.

exercises.target: کمک می‌کنم به شرطی که کار کنی
exercises.translit: kumak mēkunam ba shart-ē ke kār kuni
exercises.en: I'll help, on the condition that you work.
I'll give the book, on the condition that you read it.
exercises.translit: ketāb rā mēdiham ba shart-ē ke bukhāni

exercises.target: می‌روم به شرطی که تو بمانی
exercises.translit: mērawam ba shart-ē ke tu bumāni
exercises.en: I'll go, provided that you stay.

lessons.title: Before I go
lessons.subtitle: qabl az īnke + subjunctive
lessons.grammarPointEn: The 'before' clause qabl az īnke (before) always takes the subjunctive, even for past events: qabl az īnke burawam.

slides.title: 'Before' loves the subjunctive
slides.body: qabl az īnke (before) is always followed by the subjunctive - the event it names hasn't happened yet at that point in the story.

examples.target: قبل از اینکه بروم، نان خوردم
examples.translit: qabl az īnke burawam, nān khurdam

exercises.hint: 'Before' always takes the subjunctive.

exercises.en: Before you sleep, read the book.
exercises.translit: qabl az īnke bukhābi, ketāb bukhān

exercises.target: قبل از اینکه بروی، مرا ببین
exercises.translit: qabl az īnke burawi, marā bubīn

distractorsTarget.target: قبل از اینکه رفتی، مرا دیدی
distractorsTarget.translit: qabl az īnke rafti, marā dīdi

distractorsTarget.target: بعد از اینکه بروی، مرا ببین
distractorsTarget.translit: bād az īnke burawi, marā bubīn

exercises.target: قبل از اینکه او ___، ما آمدیم
exercises.translit: qabl az īnke ō ___, mā āmadēm

lessons.title: After it happened
lessons.subtitle: bād az īnke + past
lessons.grammarPointEn: The 'after' clause bād az īnke (after) takes the indicative past, unlike 'before': bād az īnke āmad, raftēm.

slides.title: 'After' takes the real tense
slides.body: bād az īnke (after) describes something that did happen, so it takes the ordinary past - the mirror image of 'before'.

exercises.target: بعد از اینکه نان خوردم، خوابیدم
exercises.translit: bād az īnke nān khurdam, khābīdam

exercises.hint: 'After' takes the real past, not the subjunctive.

exercises.en: After I read the book, I gave it to you.
exercises.translit: bād az īnke ketāb rā khāndam, ba tu dādam

exercises.target: بعد از اینکه کار کردم، مانده شدم
exercises.translit: bād az īnke kār kardam, mānda shudam
exercises.en: After I worked, I got tired.

distractorsTarget.target: قبل از اینکه کار کنم، مانده شدم
distractorsTarget.translit: qabl az īnke kār kunam, mānda shudam

lessons.title: Whenever
lessons.subtitle: har waqt ke and hargāh
lessons.grammarPointEn: Generalizing time with har waqt ke / hargāh (whenever), used for repeated or conditional-in-time situations.

slides.title: Any time it happens
slides.body: har waqt ke and hargāh both mean 'whenever' - the event repeats or holds any time the condition is met.

examples.target: هر وقت که می‌آیی، خوش می‌شوم
examples.translit: har waqt ke mēāyi, khush mēshawam
examples.en: Whenever you come, I am glad.

exercises.en: Whenever you come, I am glad.
Whenever I see him, I am happy.
exercises.translit: har waqt ke ō rā mēbīnam, khush mēshawam

exercises.target: هرگاه کار داری، به من بگو
exercises.translit: hargāh kār dāri, ba man bugō
exercises.en: Whenever you have work, tell me.

distractorsTarget.target: چون کار داری، به من بگو
distractorsTarget.translit: chun kār dāri, ba man bugō

distractorsTarget.target: اگرچه کار داری، به من بگو
distractorsTarget.translit: agarche kār dāri, ba man bugō

exercises.en: Whenever you want, you can come.

lessons.title: It is said that
lessons.subtitle: Impersonal reporting
lessons.grammarPointEn: Impersonal reporting with gufta mēshawad ke and mēgōyand ke (it is said that / they say that), attributing without a named source.

slides.title: No named source
slides.body: gufta mēshawad ke ('it is said that') and mēgōyand ke ('they say that') report general belief without naming who says it - common in formal and written Dari.

examples.target: گفته می‌شود که او رفته است
examples.translit: gufta mēshawad ke ō rafta ast
examples.en: It is said that he has gone.
They say that Kabul is beautiful.

exercises.target: گفته می‌شود که او رفته است
exercises.translit: gufta mēshawad ke ō rafta ast
exercises.en: It is said that he has gone.
distractorsEn: He said that he has gone.

exercises.en: They say that Kabul is beautiful.
It is said that this book is good.
exercises.translit: gufta mēshawad ke īn ketāb khōb ast

exercises.en: It is said that he came.
exercises.hint: The impersonal 'it is said' uses mēshawad.

exercises.target: می‌گویند که او معلم خوب است
exercises.translit: mēgōyand ke ō mu'allem-e khōb ast
exercises.en: They say that he is a good teacher.

distractorsTarget.target: او می‌گوید که معلم خوب است
distractorsTarget.translit: ō mēgōyad ke mu'allem-e khōb ast

distractorsTarget.target: گفتند که او معلم خوب است
distractorsTarget.translit: guftand ke ō mu'allem-e khōb ast

lessons.title: It seems that
lessons.subtitle: be nazar mērasad ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Expressing appearance with be nazar mērasad ke (it seems that) + clause, a hedge that softens a claim.

slides.title: Softening a claim
slides.body: be nazar mērasad ke ('it seems that') presents something as an impression rather than a fact - a key move in careful, formal speech.

examples.target: به نظر می‌رسد که او مانده است
examples.translit: be nazar mērasad ke ō mānda ast
examples.en: It seems that he is tired.

exercises.target: به نظر می‌رسد که او مانده است
exercises.translit: be nazar mērasad ke ō mānda ast
exercises.en: It seems that he is tired.
distractorsEn: He looks at the tired one.

exercises.en: It seems that it will rain.
It seems that he has gone home.
exercises.translit: be nazar mērasad ke ō ba khāna rafta ast

exercises.target: به نظر می‌رسد که کار سخت است
exercises.translit: be nazar mērasad ke kār sakht ast
exercises.en: It seems that the work is hard.

distractorsTarget.target: به نظر می‌رسد که کار آسان است
distractorsTarget.translit: be nazar mērasad ke kār āsān ast

exercises.target: به نظر می‌رسد ___ او خوش است
exercises.translit: be nazar mērasad ___ ō khush ast
exercises.en: It seems that he is happy.

lessons.title: Not only… but also
lessons.subtitle: na tanhā … balke
lessons.grammarPointEn: The paired structure na tanhā … balke … (ham) (not only … but also …), used to add and intensify.

slides.title: Adding with emphasis
slides.body: na tanhā (not only) opens the pair; balke (but rather / but also) completes it, often with ham (too). It raises the stakes of a statement.

examples.target: او نه تنها معلم، بلکه دوست من هم است
examples.translit: ō na tanhā mu'allem, balke dōst-e man ham ast
examples.en: He is not only a teacher, but also my friend.

exercises.target: او ___ معلم، بلکه دوست من هم است
exercises.translit: ō ___ mu'allem, balke dōst-e man ham ast
exercises.en: He is not only a teacher, but also my friend.

exercises.target: نه تنها آمد، بلکه کمک هم کرد
exercises.translit: na tanhā āmad, balke kumak ham kard
exercises.en: He not only came, but also helped.

exercises.target: نه تنها آمد، ___ کمک هم کرد
exercises.translit: na tanhā āmad, ___ kumak ham kard
exercises.en: He not only came, but also helped.
Not only Kabul, but Herat too is big.
exercises.translit: na tanhā kābul, balke herāt ham kalān ast

exercises.target: نه تنها خواند، بلکه نوشت هم
exercises.translit: na tanhā khānd, balke newesht ham
exercises.en: He not only read, but also wrote.

lessons.title: I wish I had gone
lessons.subtitle: kāsh + past perfect
lessons.grammarPointEn: Regret about the past with kāsh + past perfect: kāsh rafta būdam (I wish I had gone) - an unfulfilled past.

slides.title: Regret over the past
slides.body: For a regret about something that didn't happen, use kāsh with the past perfect: kāsh rafta būdam - 'I wish I had gone (but I didn't)'.

exercises.en: I wish I had seen him.

exercises.hint: A past regret uses the past perfect.

exercises.en: I wish I had helped him.
exercises.translit: kāsh ba ō kumak karda būdam

exercises.target: کاش آن کتاب را خوانده بودم
exercises.translit: kāsh ān ketāb rā khānda būdam
exercises.en: I wish I had read that book.

lessons.title: I thought he might have gone
lessons.subtitle: Embedded doubt about the past
lessons.grammarPointEn: Embedding doubt: a matrix verb of thinking with a past-subjunctive complement: fikr kardam ke rafta bāshad (I thought he might have gone).

slides.title: Doubt inside a thought
slides.body: When you report an uncertain guess about the past, the inner clause takes the past subjunctive: fikr kardam ke rafta bāshad.

examples.target: فکر کردم که او رفته باشد
examples.translit: fikr kardam ke ō rafta bāshad
examples.en: I thought he might have gone.

exercises.en: I thought he might have gone.

exercises.target: گمان کردم که نان خورده باشد
exercises.translit: gumān kardam ke nān khurda bāshad
exercises.en: I supposed he might have eaten.

exercises.target: فکر کردم که او رفت باشد
exercises.translit: fikr kardam ke ō raft bāshad
exercises.en: I thought he might have gone.
exercises.hint: The past subjunctive needs the participle: rafta bāshad.

exercises.en: I thought that you might have come.
exercises.translit: fikr kardam ke tu āmada bāshi

exercises.target: گمان کردم که او را دیده باشی
exercises.translit: gumān kardam ke ō rā dīda bāshi
exercises.en: I supposed you might have seen him.

distractorsTarget.target: گمان کردم که او را دیدی
distractorsTarget.translit: gumān kardam ke ō rā dīdi

distractorsTarget.target: فکر کردم که او را ببینی
distractorsTarget.translit: fikr kardam ke ō rā bubīni

pairs.en: I thought he might have gone

lessons.title: As if it were true
lessons.subtitle: gōyā and mānand-e īnke
lessons.grammarPointEn: Unreal comparison with gōyā (as if / as though) + past, presenting something contrary to fact for effect.

slides.title: gōyā - as if
slides.body: gōyā ('as if') introduces an unreal comparison, usually with a past-tense verb: 'he spoke as if he knew everything'.

exercises.en: As if he hadn't seen me.
He spoke as if he were the teacher.
As if he had heard nothing.
As if she had seen him before.

lessons.title: The formal register
lessons.subtitle: namūdan and gardīdan
lessons.grammarPointEn: Formal/written register: namūdan replaces kardan (to do) and gardīdan replaces shudan (to become) in official style.

slides.title: Elevated equivalents
slides.body: In formal writing, namūdan stands in for kardan, and gardīdan for shudan. Same meaning, higher register - you'll meet them in letters and news.

exercises.target: او خوش گردید و کار نمود
exercises.translit: ō khush gardīd wa kār namūd
exercises.en: He became happy and worked. (but check the register mix)
exercises.hint: For a simple everyday statement, shud fits better than the formal gardīd.

lessons.title: Everyday idioms
lessons.subtitle: Light-verb expressions
lessons.grammarPointEn: High-frequency idioms built on light verbs: ba yād āwardan (to remember), az dast dādan (to lose), ba dast āwardan (to obtain).

slides.title: Fixed expressions
slides.body: Many everyday meanings are idioms with a noun + light verb. ba yād āwardan - 'to bring to mind, remember'; az dast dādan - 'to give from the hand, lose'.

examples.target: نام او را به یاد آوردم
examples.translit: nām-e ō rā ba yād āwardam

examples.target: پول خود را از دست داد

exercises.translit: nām-e ō rā ba yād āwardam

dōst-e khud rā ba yād āwardam

lessons.title: C1 review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from this level, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of C1: concession, exception and stipulation, before/after/whenever clauses, impersonal reporting, 'it seems', not-only-but-also, regret, embedded doubt, 'as if', formal register, and idioms.

slides.title: You're near fluent
slides.body: You can now concede and stipulate, hedge and report impersonally, express regret and unreal comparison, and switch into a formal register. This set draws on all of it.

examples.target: گفته می‌شود که اگرچه سخت بود، باز هم کار کرد
examples.translit: gufta mēshawad ke agarche sakht būd, bāz ham kār kard
examples.en: It is said that although it was hard, he still worked.

exercises.target: چون مانده بود، باز هم کار کرد
exercises.translit: chun mānda būd, bāz ham kār kard
exercises.en: Although he was tired, he still worked.
exercises.hint: 'Although' concedes; chun means 'because'.

exercises.target: به نظر می‌رسد که او رفته باشد
exercises.translit: be nazar mērasad ke ō rafta bāshad
exercises.en: It seems that he might have gone.
distractorsEn: It is certain that he went.

exercises.en: I wish I had seen him.
I won't go unless you come.

exercises.target: او نه تنها آمد، بلکه کمک هم کرد
exercises.translit: ō na tanhā āmad, balke kumak ham kard
exercises.en: He not only came, but also helped.

lessons.title: With respect
lessons.subtitle: Formal address
lessons.grammarPointEn: Formal address and honorifics: mohtaram (respected), jenāb (sir/His Excellency), and the polite plural shumā for a single addressee in official settings.

slides.title: Speaking with deference
slides.body: In official Dari you address people with honorifics: mohtaram (respected) before a title, jenāb (sir) for high standing, and always the polite plural shumā.

exercises.en: Your Excellency, where are you going?
exercises.hint: An honorific address takes the polite plural form.

lessons.title: The bureaucratic voice
lessons.subtitle: Official verbs and passives
lessons.grammarPointEn: Bureaucratic/official style: heavy use of the passive and formal verbs (namūdan, gardīdan) to sound impersonal and authoritative.

slides.title: Impersonal authority
slides.body: Official writing prefers the passive and the formal verbs, hiding the doer: 'the letter was signed', 'the decision was made'. It sounds neutral and authoritative.

exercises.target: نامه امضا کرده شد توسط رئیس
exercises.translit: nāma emzā karda shud tawassot-e ra'īs
exercises.en: The letter was signed by the chief.
exercises.hint: 'was signed' pairs the participle with shudan, not kardan.

lessons.title: Precision in meaning
lessons.subtitle: manzūr, qasd, ma'nā
lessons.grammarPointEn: Talking about meaning and intent precisely: manzūr (what one means), qasd (intention), ma'nā (the meaning of a word) - distinguishing subtle senses.

slides.title: Meaning vs intention
slides.body: ma'nā is the meaning of a word or phrase; manzūr is what a speaker means; qasd is intention (what one plans). Precise speakers keep them apart.

examples.en: What is the meaning of this word?

exercises.en: What is the meaning of this word?
I don't know the meaning of this word.
What is the meaning of this word?
exercises.hint: A word has a ma'nā (meaning); qasd is a person's intention.

lessons.title: The emphatic self
lessons.subtitle: khud and its weight
lessons.grammarPointEn: Emphatic and reflexive khud: khudam āmadam (I myself came), khud-e ra'īs (the chief himself); doubling for strong emphasis.

slides.title: …himself, …myself
slides.body: khud plus a possessive gives emphasis: khudam (myself), khud-e ō (himself). Placed by the subject, it stresses 'that very one, in person'.

exercises.en: The chief himself signed the letter.

lessons.title: Fronting for effect
lessons.subtitle: Marked word order
lessons.grammarPointEn: Marked word order: moving an object or adverb to the front for emphasis, keeping the verb final: īn ketāb rā man khāndam (THIS book, I read).

slides.title: Put the focus first
slides.body: Dari usually runs subject–object–verb, but you can front the element you want to stress. 'This book, I read' puts the spotlight on the book.

distractorsEn: This is the book I write.

exercises.hint: Even when fronted, the verb agrees with the subject 'I'.

lessons.title: Heavy noun phrases
lessons.subtitle: Long ezafe chains
lessons.grammarPointEn: Reading long ezāfa chains that stack modifiers and possessors: ketāb-e naw-e mu'allem-e mektab-e mā (our school's teacher's new book).

slides.title: Following the chain
slides.body: Formal Dari builds long ezāfa chains, each -e linking to the next. Read them from the head noun outward: 'book - new - of the teacher - of our school'.

examples.en: The new book of our school's teacher.

exercises.en: The new book of our school's teacher.
distractorsEn: The teacher of our new book's school.

exercises.en: The door of my father's house.
The name of my brother's good friend.
distractorsEn: The good name of my brother's friend.

exercises.en: My brother's new book is beautiful.

lessons.title: Words of wisdom
lessons.subtitle: Proverbs
lessons.grammarPointEn: Understanding common proverbs (zarb-ul-masal) whose meaning is figurative rather than literal.

slides.title: Meaning beyond the words
slides.body: Proverbs carry a lesson under a literal picture. Learn a few common ones and their intended sense.

examples.en: Drop by drop it becomes a river. (small efforts add up)

exercises.en: Small efforts add up over time.
distractorsEn: A drop cannot fill a river.

exercises.target: کار امروز را به فردا نکن
exercises.translit: kār-e emrōz rā ba fardā nakun
exercises.en: Don't leave today's work for tomorrow.

pairs.en: a book is the best friend

distractorsEn: Time is money to buy gold.

exercises.en: Drop by drop it becomes a river.
Better to arrive late but do it right.

lessons.title: The language of the body
lessons.subtitle: Idioms with dil, dast, sar
lessons.grammarPointEn: Figurative idioms built on body parts: dil (heart) for feeling, dast (hand) for action/possession, sar (head) for mind/beginning.

slides.title: Body parts, big meanings
slides.body: dil (heart) carries emotion, dast (hand) carries action or having, sar (head) carries thought. dilam mēkhāhad - 'my heart wants', i.e. 'I feel like'.

exercises.target: روز را به کار به سر برد
exercises.translit: rōz rā ba kār ba sar burd
distractorsEn: He carried work on his head.
He worked for a day's pay.

exercises.hint: 'To feel like' uses dil (heart), not sar (head).

lessons.title: Figurative light verbs
lessons.subtitle: Metaphor in everyday verbs
lessons.grammarPointEn: Light-verb expressions with figurative meaning: ba dast āwardan (to gain), az dast dādan (to lose), ba kār burdan (to employ/use).

slides.title: Verbs that carry images
slides.body: Many abstract meanings ride on concrete verbs. ba dast āwardan (bring to hand) = 'gain'; ba kār burdan (carry to work) = 'use/apply'.

exercises.target: این کلمه را در نوشته خود به کار ___
exercises.translit: īn kalema rā dar neweshta-ye khud ba kār ___
exercises.en: He used this word in his writing.

lessons.title: On one hand, on the other
lessons.subtitle: Balancing two sides
lessons.grammarPointEn: Weighing arguments with az yak sū / az yak taraf … az sū-ye dīgar / az taraf-e dīgar (on one hand … on the other).

slides.title: Two sides of a case
slides.body: To present balanced views, open with az yak sū (on one hand) and answer with az sū-ye dīgar (on the other). It signals fair, structured argument.

examples.target: از یک سو خوب است، از سوی دیگر گران است
examples.translit: az yak sū khōb ast, az sū-ye dīgar gerān ast
examples.en: On one hand it's good, on the other it's expensive.

exercises.target: ___ خوب است، از سوی دیگر گران است
exercises.translit: ___ khōb ast, az sū-ye dīgar gerān ast
exercises.en: On one hand it's good, on the other it's expensive.

exercises.target: از یک طرف آسان، از طرف دیگر خطرناک است
exercises.translit: az yak taraf āsān, az taraf-e dīgar khatarnāk ast
exercises.en: On one hand easy, on the other dangerous.
distractorsEn: One way is dangerous and hard.

exercises.en: On one hand he is tired, on the other he is happy.
exercises.translit: az yak sū mānda ast, az sū-ye dīgar khush ast

exercises.en: In any case, we are going.

exercises.target: از یک سو ارزان، ___ خراب است
exercises.translit: az yak sū arzān, ___ kharāb ast
exercises.en: On one hand cheap, on the other broken.

lessons.title: Hedging your claim
lessons.subtitle: ehtemālan, ba gumān-e man
lessons.grammarPointEn: Marking stance and probability: ehtemālan (probably), ba gumān-e man (in my opinion), ba har hāl (in any case).

slides.title: How sure are you?
slides.body: Careful writers mark how strongly they claim something: ehtemālan (probably), ba gumān-e man (in my view). These soften or frame an assertion.

examples.target: به گمان من، این درست است
examples.translit: ba gumān-e man, īn durust ast
examples.en: In my opinion, this is right.

exercises.target: به گمان من، این درست است
exercises.translit: ba gumān-e man, īn durust ast
exercises.en: In my opinion, this is right.
distractorsEn: I am sure this is wrong.
In his opinion, this is right.

exercises.hint: 'Probably' is ehtemālan; hargez means 'never'.

exercises.en: In my opinion, the work is hard.

lessons.title: Layered concession
lessons.subtitle: Stacking counter-arguments
lessons.grammarPointEn: Building a nuanced argument by stacking concession and result: agarche … amā … bā īn ham … (although … but … even so …).

slides.title: Grant, counter, conclude
slides.body: A sophisticated argument concedes a point (agarche), counters it (amā), and still concludes (bā īn ham / bāz ham). Layering these shows control.

examples.target: اگرچه سخت بود، اما با این هم موفق شد
examples.translit: agarche sakht būd, amā bā īn ham muwaffaq shud
examples.en: Although it was hard, but even so he succeeded.

exercises.target: اگرچه سخت بود، اما با این هم کرد
exercises.translit: agarche sakht būd, amā bā īn ham kard
exercises.en: Although it was hard, even so he did it.
distractorsEn: Because it was hard, he did it.
It was hard, so he didn't do it.

exercises.target: اگرچه مانده بود، اما ___ کار کرد
exercises.translit: agarche mānda būd, amā ___ kār kard
exercises.en: Although he was tired, even so he worked.
Although he was sick, even so he came.
exercises.translit: agarche marīz būd, bā īn ham āmad

exercises.target: اگرچه پول نداشت، با این هم کتاب خرید
exercises.translit: agarche pūl nadāsht, bā īn ham ketāb kharīd
exercises.en: Although he had no money, even so he bought a book.
Although it was cold, even so we went.
exercises.hint: After 'although', the answer is 'even so', not 'therefore'.

lessons.title: Precise time reference
lessons.subtitle: hanōz, tā ba hāl, dēgar
lessons.grammarPointEn: Fine time reference: hanōz (still / not yet), tā ba hāl (until now, with the perfect), and dēgar in the sense of 'no longer'.

slides.title: Still, yet, no longer
slides.body: hanōz + negative = 'not yet'; tā ba hāl + perfect = 'until now'; dēgar + negative = 'no longer'. Small words, precise meanings.

exercises.target: تا به حال او را ندیده‌ام
exercises.translit: tā ba hāl ō rā nadīda-am
exercises.en: Until now I haven't seen him.

exercises.hint: 'Not yet' is hanōz; dēgar means 'no longer'.

lessons.title: Switching register in context
lessons.subtitle: Reading the situation
lessons.grammarPointEn: Choosing register by situation: familiar tu and simple verbs with friends; polite shumā, honorifics and formal verbs in official or written contexts.

slides.title: Match your words to the room
slides.body: Near-native command means switching register smoothly: casual with friends (tu, kardan), formal with officials or in writing (shumā, namūdan, honorifics). Reading which fits is the final skill.

examples.en: To a friend: come, let's go.

exercises.en: Tell your friend: come, let's go.

exercises.hint: An honorific address needs the formal 'please come'.

exercises.en: To the respected teacher: please sit.

lessons.title: C2 review
lessons.subtitle: The whole language, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of C2: formal address and register, official style, meaning nuance, emphatic and fronted structures, ezāfa chains, proverbs and idioms, balanced argument, hedging, layered concession, and precise time reference.

slides.title: You've done it
slides.body: From your first pronoun to layered argument and register-switching - you now command the whole ladder. This final set mixes the C2 toolkit. تبریک!

examples.translit: agarche sakht būd, amā bā īn ham ba hadaf-e khud rasīd
examples.en: Although it was hard, even so he reached his goal.

exercises.en: Your Excellency, where are you going?
exercises.hint: An honorific address takes the polite plural.

exercises.target: از یک سو ارزان، از سوی دیگر خراب است
exercises.translit: az yak sū arzān, az sū-ye dīgar kharāb ast
exercises.en: On one hand cheap, on the other broken.
distractorsEn: One side is broken and dear.

exercises.en: He has probably not come yet.
Although it was cold, even so we went.
